title: Graphical LP solution and solution types

sections.heading: The idea

sections.body_md:
A linear program in two variables can be settled with a sketch. Each constraint is a half-plane. The feasible set is their intersection: a polygon, a ray, a line, an empty set, or some unbounded convex piece of the plane. The objective \(c^T x\) has level lines that are parallel, and the gradient \(c\) points toward larger values.

Slide a level line across the feasible set in the direction that decreases the objective, and stop at the last contact. One contact point is a unique minimizer. Contact along a whole edge means every point of that edge is optimal, and they share one optimal value. If the line can travel forever while still touching the set, the objective is unbounded below. If the intersection was empty to begin with, there is no contact and the program is infeasible.

An unbounded feasible set is not the same fact as an unbounded objective. A cost that points back toward the set can still attain a minimum on an unbounded region. The picture separates those two outcomes, and it also separates a unique vertex optimum from an edge of optima.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: A level of \(p x + q y\) is the line \(p x + q y = c\). If \(q \ne 0\), the slope is \(-p/q\). The four outcomes for a linear objective on a convex planar set are: a unique minimizer, a whole convex piece of minimizers (often an edge), an unbounded objective, and an empty feasible set. On a nonempty polygon the minimum and the maximum are attained, and each is attained at an extreme point. The optimal value is one number even when several points attain it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A shed floor is the triangle with vertices \((7, 11)\), \((15, 11)\), and \((7, 18)\). Minimize \(x + y\). The vertex values are \(7 + 11 = 18\), \(15 + 11 = 26\), and \(7 + 18 = 25\).

The shed level is 18, attained only at \((7, 11)\). The other two vertices are worse, so the minimizer is unique. The same three numbers also show that the maximum on this triangle is 26. Nothing in the interior can beat a vertex for this linear cost, because a value strictly inside the range of the vertices is a convex combination of vertex values.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Reading an interior point, or the centroid of a polygon, as the optimum is the common miss. A nonconstant linear function on a convex set is never minimized in the relative interior. A second miss is to treat an unbounded feasible set as an unbounded program without looking at the cost direction. A third is to report one endpoint of an optimal edge and forget the rest of the edge. The optimal value is still unique.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The reason a vertex wins is that a linear function on a polyhedron attains its bounds at extreme points, when it attains them at all. Those extreme points are the basic feasible solutions once the program is written with equalities and nonnegative variables. The algebra that walks from one such point to a neighboring one is the simplex iteration. The picture in the plane is the same walk, seen without a tableau.
